The post WEEKEND READING: Part Two: From loneliness to belonging: what can universities actually do? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Dr David Gilani, Head of Access and Participation, Middlesex University and Dr Michelle Morgan, Dean of Students, University of East London.

Pre-arrival Academic Questionnaire Pilot data, drawn from over 7,800 new students across fifteen English institutions, confirmed what many of us working in higher education have long suspected: transitioning into university leaves many students reporting frequent loneliness.

Following on from our first blog, which explored how loneliness on entry varies across domicile, sex, age, disability, ethnicity, prior school attendance and care and estrangement status, this blog turns to what universities can do about it. And just as importantly, what should we be careful not to get wrong? Here are five assumptions about loneliness and belonging that the sector is at risk of making, and five practical steps that institutions can take that mitigate these risks.

Risk one – assuming that loneliness is a failure

Feeling some level of loneliness, especially during a time of significant change to one’s life, identity and social relationships, is completely normal. As Dr Gareth Hughes puts it when talking about overcoming loneliness at university , ‘loneliness is a normal human response to the absence of something we need, like feeling hungry when we need food’. It is a warning sign that we need to act to improve our social connections, rather than a sign that something is broken. The scale of what part one found reinforces this: across the pilot, feeling lonely was consistently the most cited experience under the ‘often’ response, and it showed up across every student characteristic we looked at. Students who report feeling lonely before they have even arrived are experiencing the predictable consequence of a significant social transition, not a personal failing.

This matters because of how institutions tend to respond to loneliness data. The instinct is often to treat it as a problem to be solved, but this can lead to interventions that stigmatise further: inadvertently signalling to students that feeling lonely means they were not cut out for university. A student who still feels disconnected in week six may conclude that the problem is with them.

Jim Dickinson has argued persuasively on Wonkhe that many institutional approaches to belonging risk getting the social psychology the wrong way around – focusing on deficits in particular student groups rather than on the conditions that make connection normal for everyone. The loneliness data reinforces the importance of that distinction. The goal is not to fix lonely students. It is to build the scaffolding within which students can act to connect i.e. creating the conditions that enable an individual to actively get involved and engage with the school, community or culture.

Risk two – assuming that belonging is a destination

One of the consistent findings in the research literature is that belonging is not like a light switch that you flick on or off. It fluctuates, constantly changing over time. It operates differently at different points in the year and across different aspects of a student’s life and identity – their course, their campus, their friendships, their home community, etc.

This creates a timing problem. Students arrive lonely and so institutions respond with a burst of front-loaded support: welcome events, induction programmes, peer mentoring, academic support interventions. However then, broadly speaking as term progresses, these supportive structures dissipate.

Longitudinal research on belonging is still under-utilised, but the studies that track it over time tend to find belonging decreasing as the first-year progresses. A student who looks fine in a week-four survey may be in a very different place by January. If we front-load everything into establishing belonging early and then forget the rest of the journey, we miss the students who need support at exactly the moment we have stopped paying attention.

This matters more given the changing profile of the student body. Students coming through clearing or different entry points throughout the year; non-UK students who miss early induction due to visa and travel delays; those with work and caring responsibilities; and younger undergraduates navigating the transition for the first time all have most to lose when belonging work is front-loaded into the opening weeks.

Risk three – assuming that one source of connection addresses all loneliness

Recent analysis from Wonkhe of over 18,000 students across the UK found that over four in ten students who report a strong sense of belonging are also frequently lonely. However, a single measure of loneliness, or of belonging, will not capture the full picture, because students report many different aspects of connection and disconnection at once.

This maps onto a distinction that loneliness researchers draw between social loneliness (the absence of a broader network or group to belong to) and emotional loneliness (the absence of close individual attachments). A student who arrives lonely but quickly finds a flatmate or friends through a student society may have addressed some of what was making them feel lonely. But they may still feel that something is missing if they have not found connection within their course of study – the relationships that make classes, assessments and the route towards a discipline-relevant career feel accessible. The Wonkhe report calls this ‘academic citizenship’: the sense of knowing how to navigate your programme, feeling confident about where your studies are heading, and feeling free to speak in seminars. Students who have only made friends outside their subject area can show up fine on some belonging measures, while their career confidence and willingness to participate academically are often lower.

Risk four – assuming that our governance structures are fit for all students’ needs

Part one showed that among care-experienced undergraduates, over half (50.7%) reported lacking companionship at least some of the time, compared to 38.2% of their peers. Estranged undergraduates were more than twice as likely to report often feeling lonely (22.2%) compared to non-estranged students (13.4%). This is consistent with the Unite Foundation’s deep dive into the academic experience of estranged and care-experienced students.

Universities know this, and there has been notable progress from institutions and sector charities alike, from bursaries and funded accommodation through the Unite Foundation to the growing number of institutions signing up to charter-marks like the Care Leavers Covenant.

However, while there is greater provision and action to support care-experienced students, the vast majority of institutions do not have formal targets for these students, often because numbers are too small to have found significant differences in outcomes. Analysis of access and participation plans across England finds only 22 targets focused specifically on care-experienced students (Figure 1). The risk here is therefore that institutions, and the sector, are not set up to track whether all this action is actually leading to improvements in access, success and progression for care-experienced students.

Risk five – assuming that we need to wait until ‘induction’ to address student loneliness

The inverse relationship between prior school attendance and pre-arrival loneliness is one of the most striking findings that we discussed in our first blog on the pre-arrival loneliness data. What’s most troubling is that the number of school children classed as severely absent from school has been rising since the pandemic – with 150,000 now meeting that threshold.

Universities cannot solve school attendance directly, but we can indirectly through our outreach work and activities. At its best, these efforts help to create a clearer link for young people between staying in education and realising the future that they want. In the recent ‘From the Boys’ project at Middlesex University, listening to the experiences and perspectives of teenage boys in North London schools has highlighted how many do not see education as connected to how they define success.

If that belief is shaping attendance decisions, and attendance is shaping the loneliness that students feel in the transition to university, then access and outreach work that addresses those motivational questions is doing belonging work before students even set foot on campus. Alex Blower’s Boys Impact group has been developing practical approaches to this nationally, and it is worth universities asking whether their outreach strategies appropriately consider improved attendance (either as an end in itself or a means to improved student wellbeing later in students’ educational journey).

It is worth noting that the higher pre-arrival loneliness in part one was reported by female rather than male undergraduates, a reminder that single demographic binaries can hide a lot even where the national access picture points the other way.

So, what can universities actually do?

Part one of this blog clearly established that loneliness is pervasive on entry into higher education, and at risk of increasing given the links with school absence. Hopefully, from reading the risks above, colleagues will have ideas of how these can be mitigated and flipped into different approaches to address student loneliness and build belonging. Below is a summary of five suggestions that can assist with this:

1. Treat outreach as belonging work

Pre-arrival loneliness tracks with prior school attendance, which tells us the belonging journey starts well before enrolment. Outreach that builds credible connections between education and young people’s own aspirations is doing preventive work, but only if it listens to how pupils themselves define success rather than assuming that definition for them.

2. Plan for transition points after the initial induction period

Universities and students’ unions are generally good at inclusive welcome approaches, but these are front-loaded and rarely matched by plans for when students move between modules, accommodation and academic years. The students who most need support are often those for whom welcome and orientation never lands, because they arrived through clearing, missed early weeks due to visa delays, or were managing caring responsibilities. Extend welcome beyond the first week and create a full programme of induction to study (across the first term), and put similar support around later transition points where the risk of loneliness rises again.

3. Invest in subject-level community, together with your students’ union

Community-building tends to be organised around the institution, through big events and campus-wide societies. But the evidence suggests the unit that matters most for academic belonging is the subject discipline, and that is where universities and students’ unions need to work together. Plenty of lessons to be learned here from our continental European counterparts.

4. Measure belonging and connection in more than one way

A single survey, whether pre-arrival or at week four, will miss both the belonging dip that comes later in the first year and the four in ten students who say they belong while still feeling frequently lonely. Distinguishing social from emotional loneliness, and academic citizenship from social belonging, gives a more honest picture, which means being comfortable with data from multiple sources that sometimes tell conflicting stories.

5. Fill the gaps in formal accountability mechanisms and targets

The sector knows the barriers faced by care-experienced and estranged students and is making progress, but formal reporting takes time to catch up. Only 22 formal targets across Access and Participation Plans relate to these groups. Institutions that develop their own updated targets have a better chance of measuring whether their support is actually working.

title: Students scramble for accommodation after provider goes bust in Dundee
summary:
Case highlights severe financial strain on sector across UK as string of university housing schemes fail

  • Are you having problems with your accommodation provider?

Nearly 70 students in Dundee have been left scrambling to find accommodation for this academic year after the latest in a string of university housing schemes went bust amid severe financial strain on the sector.

Students in the city have been forced to find alternative housing and rapidly move their possessions as term begins this month after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a city centre block.

Continue reading...
full_text:
Nearly 70 students in Dundee have been left scrambling to find accommodation for this academic year after the latest in a string of university housing schemes went bust amid severe financial strain on the sector.

Students in the city have been forced to find alternative housing and rapidly move their possessions as term begins this month after the collapse of the owner of Marketgait Apartments, a city centre block.

The company filed for administration in mid-July with 68 rooms let. Just weeks earlier it had been urging students to quickly secure its “perfect homes” in online marketing.

It is further evidence of a crisis in the UK student housing sector, with companies going bust or disposing of properties owing to to a combination of poor demand or oversupply in different regions.

Accommodation providers are grappling with falling international student numbers, down for a third year; a cost of living squeeze; and higher borrowing and build costs, exacerbated by the Iran war, affecting upgrades at older properties.

While domestic student numbers are at a record high, a growing proportion live at home, mostly because of the cost of renting, in what has been called “the rise of the commuter student”.

A boom in new-build student housing in recent years led to too many tower blocks in places such as Coventry, Leeds and Nottingham. Glasgow, Bristol and London still face shortages, with a general lack of affordable rooms.

Modern, purpose-built housing tends to command higher rents than student halls on campus or private rooms, and is out of reach for many domestic students, with wealthier overseas students the main occupants.

Three weeks before the then owners filed for administration, Marketgait Apartments in Dundee was still being promoted to students.

The 116-room building, less than 10-minute walk from Abertay and Dundee universities, had a concierge and a shared lounge with a pool table. The weekly rent was pitched at £199 for a studio and £165 for an en suite room.

“Looking for your perfect student home in Dundee?” the operator, Prestige Student Living, wrote on Facebook on 23 June. “Marketgait Apartments still have rooms available – but not for long! Secure your spot today and avoid missing out on a prime location, modern living, and everything you need right on your doorstep. Book now before it’s gone!”

On 15 July, however, partners from FRP Advisory were appointed to the Jersey-based special purpose vehicle that owns the redbrick block after its owners, the real estate manager 90 North and Kuwaiti investment company Rasameel, failed to repay a £5.7m loan against the property.

Falling student numbers at the building led to financial losses, leaving the company unable to fund essential fire safety remedial works. The building remains closed while its new owner, ATK Property, carries out the work.

James Elliot, 21, who recently graduated from Dundee university, said he knew people living in Margetgait who had to move out and were “anxious, stressed and shocked”.

“A lot of the students had contracts to stay there next year, but they were just told they had to leave in a month, you need to be out, you need to move your things out.” Students were helped to book alternative accommodation.

Elliot, a housing activist and member of Scotland’s tenants’ and community union Living Rent, added: “Because so many international students were away back home, they couldn’t do that in person. They had all of their belongings there for next year, clothes, pots and pans, everything they needed for uni. So they had to pay a fee for a third party to store their things for them.”

Prestige said the lets in place when Marketgait went into administration included 27 students who had renewed their contracts for the 2026-27 academic year. Of those, 17 had already moved out for the summer. Six others asked Prestige for details of a moving company and paid for it themselves.

A Prestige spokesperson said the decision and subsequent closure was beyond the managing agent’s control. “Our team took immediate action to notify students, help them secure alternative accommodation in Dundee and return all payments made to us. We deeply sympathise with the students affected by the news and will continue to do all we can to support them.”

This is the latest failure in the sector. Amare Students, which ran a 64-room student accommodation block in Birmingham, went into administration in January. Alma Place, a 393-room block in Belfast, was acquired by London-based investors the same month, just over a year after going into receivership.

Several struggling housing providers have sought planning permission to open up their buildings to non-students, including a 91-room block in Coventry that is in receivership. Receivers want to let 50 rooms to city workers instead of students.

Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, is accelerating a programme of selling off unwanted blocks, with 15,000 to 20,000 beds earmarked for sale, after it slumped to a £418m loss in the first half of the year. Its portfolio will slim down to 55,000-60,000 beds in 20 cities, compared with 29 at present, “to increase alignment to the UK’s strongest universities, where student demand is robust and growing”.

title: Canadian language school files for bankruptcy, leaving students stranded
summary: A notice posted to the International Language Academy of Canada's website says it has ceased operations effective immediately and cancelled all classes.
full_text:
Canada's largest private language school filed for bankruptcy on Friday, leaving current and incoming students in limbo.

A notice posted to the International Language Academy of Canada's (ILAC) website says it has ceased operations effective immediately, noting it "no longer has the financial resources necessary to continue operating."

ILAC operated in Vancouver and Toronto, offering a variety of programs including short-term English-language courses, a high school program, and college programs lasting up to two years.

"I’m just really confused and lost," said incoming student José Carlos Chavez, speaking from Guadalajara, Mexico, on Saturday.

Chavez, who works in Mexico as a professional photographer, was supposed to be starting a two-year-long marketing program at ILAC in mid-October.

His flight to Vancouver is booked for next week.

Chavez says he found out the news from social media. Despite reaching out to the school, he says he has not yet heard back from ILAC directly.

According to receipts Chavez provided to CBC News, he has paid the school almost $14,000 in tuition fees.

He will also have to pay a penalty if he cancels his Vancouver apartment lease now — which will cost him around $1,800.

"Stressed, confused, I don’t know what’s going to happen," said Chavez.

Chavez worries he may have to go into debt and won’t be able to afford studying elsewhere if he doesn’t receive a refund.

"I just hope that the school can ... help me in any possible way," he said.

The school's notice says it has faced financial challenges over the past three years due to "significant regulatory changes affecting the sector."

Since the federal government started tightening the intake cap on international student permit applications, education providers have been challenged by funding issues.

The number of new students arriving in Canada with study permits has dropped from roughly 293,000 in 2024 to 115,000 in 2025. Between January and July this year, only about 28,000 new students came to Canada with study permits.

Languages Canada, the national language education association that represents and accredits language programs, said the school has 1,362 students.

"The sudden and disorderly closure of Canada’s largest language school is a shock to everyone," said a Saturday statement from the organization’s executive director Gonzalo Peralta.

The statement said Languages Canada will work over the weekend to place current students in alternate equivalent programs.

Incoming students face the unknown

Beatriz Gil runs Truly Canadian Education, a company based in Metro Vancouver that connects international students to Canadian schooling.

She has dozens of clients currently enrolled in ILAC programs in Vancouver and Toronto. For both students and staff, she says Friday was a confusing and upsetting day.

"We were in shock," Gil said, noting she got a call from an ILAC staff member in tears.

Gil said those who were studying at the ILAC high school in Vancouver were asked to take their items and leave the building on Friday.

"They were outside the school with all their belongings asking what’s going on?" she said.

She said their team is working with Languages Canada to transfer current students to other institutions in Vancouver and Toronto.

But for incoming students like Chavez, Gil says she does not know what will happen.

Gil said she is working with one incoming student who had just made her tuition payment to the institution on Thursday — the day before it declared bankruptcy.

"It’s very, very sad for all of them," she said.

ILAC's closure comes just five days after the closure of EC English, a major international English-language school that had operations in Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal.

"Indeed, there have been closures of many language programs around the world in the last few years," said Language Canada's statement on the ILAC closure.

title: In a first, abetment FIR filed against IIT-Bombay professor in student’s death
summary: An IIT-Bombay professor faces accusations following a student's death by suicide on campus.  The student's parents alleged casteist remarks and harassment by the professor.  Police have transferred the case to the crime branch for further investigation.  The institute stated no disciplinary action was initiated against the student.  The family refused to claim the body until the accused were arrested.
full_text:
Sahil Wakode, IIT-Bombay student who died by suicide on Friday with his parents claiming 'harassment'

MUMBAI: In possibly the first such instance, an IIT-Bombay professor was named an accused in connection with a student’s death by suicide on campus on Saturday. Powai police also applied provisions of the Prevention of Atrocities Act after a specific complaint was made by the parents of the student, Sahil Wakode, that he was being harassed with “casteist remarks”. Late on Saturday, the case was transferred to the crime branch for investigation.This is the third incident of suicide on the campus this year. On Friday, Wakode (20), a second-year student in the energy science section, was caught using a mobile phone during an examination conducted between 2 pm and 4 pm. He had allegedly uploaded the exam question paper on an AI platform to seek answers. He was subsequently found dead in his hostel room. Prof Suryanarayana Doolla from the energy science department, named in the FIR, was the invigilator during this exam. He was also the institute’s Dean of Student Affairs in the recent past. Besides Doolla, the FIR mentions “other senior officials” and “other officials concerned”. Commenting on the contents of the FIR, Prof Shireesh Kedare, director, IIT Bombay, denied the existence of caste-based discrimination on campus, whether in day-to-day functioning or in the administration’s or professors’ approach. “And there is absolutely none in this case. In fact, caste-based information of every student is completely hidden and not available for anybody’s information.” Wakode’s parents and some of the students alleged that the professor had taken him out of the exam hall and threatened him with suspension. But in a statement, IIT-Bombay said that “no disciplinary action was initiated against the student”. Wakode’s parents — Ravindra, an office-bearer with a multipurpose cooperative society, and Sonali, a govt school teacher — refused to claim their son’s body from the post-mortem centre at Rajawadi Hospital for over seven hours on Saturday. “I will not conduct the final rites of my son till the accused persons are arrested,” said Ravindra. Wakode was their only child. As the standoff continued, senior IPS officers reached the hospital and tried to persuade the couple to claim the body, assuring them that action would be taken on their complaint. “There have been several suicide cases in the past, with three being reported this year alone. No action has been taken against the institute or its officials. Such cases never reach a logical conclusion; no permanent solution comes out. I have lost my son, but I do not want any other child to be victimised,” said Ravindra. The couple eventually claimed the body late at night after police assured them that the investigation had been transferred to the crime branch. An ACP-rank officer from the crime branch will be conducting the probe. In his statement, which is part of the FIR, Ravindra alleged that after entering the second year, his son had told him about facing harassment from Doolla for three months. The family, however, did not file a complaint with the institute at that time. The institute’s SC/ST cell, in an email sent to students, said it had not received any complaint from Wakode alleging caste-based discrimination. Wakode’s mother, Sonali, said the family had visited him on the IIT-Bombay campus over the weekend. They had also spoken to him for half an hour on Thursday night, when he appeared to be his usual self and showed no signs of distress. “It was a regular chat. He told us he was preparing for the exam. He was not at all stressed,” said Sonali. On Friday, his father tried calling him around 5 pm, assuming his exam would have ended by then, but the call went unanswered. Wakode’s parents were informed of his death around 8 pm, first by the institute and then by Powai police. There are conflicting accounts of what happened after Wakode was found with a phone during the exam. IIT-Bombay has maintained that no disciplinary action was initiated against him and that he was counselled and assured that the incident would not adversely affect his academic career. Students, however, have alleged that Wakode was threatened with suspension. As per IIT rules, if students are found with any gadgets during the exam, they can be suspended for a semester. The institute postponed the mid-semester exams scheduled for Saturday, with protests continuing through the weekend. Advocate Nikhil Kamble, representing Wakode’s family, said the state should provide a special public prosecutor and conduct a speedy trial. He also demanded an immediate release of compensation under the provisions of the SC/ST Act to the victim’s family. An IIT-Bombay spokesperson said that the police have registered a case and the matter is under investigation and that IIT-Bombay will cooperate fully with the authorities and requested everyone to respect the family’s privacy. “We ask that people refrain from speculation as the investigation proceeds,” the spokesperson added.

End of Article

title: ‘System’ run by Modi prefers andhbhakts over students who ask questions, says Rahul Gandhi
summary: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi says students pose a danger to the ‘system’, the top layer of which he said consisted of six people, as they question why institutions like judiciary, bureaucracy and the Election Commission ‘are not doing their jobs properly’
full_text:
The “system” running the country does not want students as they raise questions, but wants only andhbhakts (blind followers), Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi said in an address to students on Saturday (September 19, 2026). The Congress refers to staunch BJP followers as andhbhakts.

Speaking at the fifth ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ student interaction programme in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, Mr. Gandhi alleged that a “system” had captured the country and was against students and the education system. He said the “system” was being controlled by a handful of powerful people, but students posed a danger to it as they raised questions.

Mr. Gandhi said he had held the ‘Chhatron Ki Goonj’ event in cities like Kota, Pune, Dehradun and Prayagraj, raising students’ issues such as paper leaks, institutional failure, infrastructural collapse and privatisation. “In Indore, we have decided that we will talk about the ‘system’ vs students today,” he said, addressing thousands of youth at Indore’s IDA ground.

“The system has various layers. At the top, there are six people. The system is run by [Prime Minister] Narendra Modiji. The tasks of threatening and beating up students with a nail-studded baton and pellet guns are done by [Union Home Minister] Amit Shah ji; he is the enforcer,” Mr. Gandhi said, displaying pictures of several BJP and RSS leaders, top bureaucrats, industrialists and media and film personalities.

‘Top layer of the system’

The top layer of the alleged system, he said, included Mr. Modi, Mr. Shah, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat, National Security Adviser Ajit Doval, and industrialists Gautam Adani and Mukesh Ambani.

The Congress MP further accused Mr. Doval of digital spying on people by tapping phones and social media.

“Ajit Doval says in informal conversation that ‘if you want to control India, you just have to control 500 people’. He has captured India’s communication. He gets phones tapped and provides information to Amit Shah ji and Narendra Modi ji. Doval is sitting in mine and your phones,” he says.

Mr. Gandhi also charged that RSS sarsanghchalak Mohan Bhagwat brought ideology to the table and in return, “crores of rupees are given to his organisation to run educational institutions”.

He alleged that industrialist Gautam Adani “finances” the system and “channels the money” earned through government contracts.

“All that money is channeled and given to the BJP for Narendra Modi ji’s marketing and to run the ‘system’,” he said.

‘Capture of institutions’

“Below this layer, there are different people who have captured every institution, like politics, business, judiciary, bureaucracy, education, media, entertainment and sports. The ‘system’ has placed its people in every institution,” he said.

“For example, the ‘system’ has given the entire contract of cricket to Amit Shah’s son [Jay Shah] despite the country having many cricket players. They have divided all the institutions among them like this,” he said.

Mr. Gandhi further said that the students posed a danger to the “system” as they questioned why institutions like judiciary, bureaucracy and the Election Commission “are not doing their jobs properly”.

“This is why the ‘system’ does not want students. It wants andhbhakts who are anti-students. It prepares and promotes andhbhakts. While students are curious, the andhbhakts are delusional and live in their own world. While students talk about love and respect, the andhbhakts spread hatred. While students are humble and listen to others, the andhbhakts are filled with arrogance. While students are fearless, the andhbhakts are cowards. While students respect women, the andhbhakts are patriarchal and attack women. While students are honest, the andhbhakts are dishonest and liars,” he said.

Mr. Gandhi claimed that those who run the “system” did not want their children to become andhbhkts and sent them to study abroad.

He also claimed that more than one lakh schools had been shut across the country and that 55% of them were in Uttar Pradesh and Madhya Pradesh alone. He claimed that the Union government’s education budget allocation had come down from 4.6% of total budget outlay in 2014 to 2.6% in 2026.

Many students and government job aspirants who were called on to the stage raised issues faced in Madhya Pradesh, including delayed recruitment to government jobs, the holding of government vacancies due to the sub judice OBC reservation hike case and delay in holding nursing exams, which has prompted students to protest.

The family of Arpit Jaj, an 18-year-old student from Dewas who died in the Delhi building collapse earlier this month, also met Mr. Gandhi on the stage and alleged that their son had died due to the “system’s failure”.

“This is the cost of not having the infrastructure and cutting down on government’s [education] budget,” he said after meeting Jaj’s family.

Students vs andhbhakts

As Mr. Gandhi pitted the students against “andhbhakts”, he said that the students were the future of India, and no country could become strong without them.

“We want that the hope in your hearts that has broken comes back fast once again; you start believing in education, and the system; and the country should run with the force of your strengths and qualities — curiosity, honesty, compassion and love,” he said.

“The students can erase the hate and violence going on in the country. Only the students can do it; the andhbhakts can never erase it. We want an India of students, not of andhbhakts. We don’t want an India of arrogance, hate and violence. We want to hear your voice. Never forget that you are the future of this country,” Mr. Gandhi said, concluding his address.

Earlier, on Saturday (September 19, 2026) morning, several posters which appeared to mock Mr. Gandhi with words like ‘Jhooth Ki Goonj’ surfaced across Indore, adding to a list of controversies that erupted in the run-up to the event.

This prompted Congress national general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh to allege that the BJP government of Madhya Pradesh was “terrified” of the event and “tried every trick in the book to stop this program”.

title: Chimica e farmaceutica lanciano un’analsul lavoro e la svolta tecnologica
summary: Lo studio verrà realizzato dall’Università degli Studi di Milano. I risultati saranno lo spunto per gli Stati generali delle relazioni industriali del settore. Buzzella: «Vogliamo anticipare i fenomeni» - Cattani: «Velocità di adattamento per la competitività»
full_text:
Per capire le trasformazioni del mercato del lavoro non resta che chiedere ai lavoratori e alle imprese come le stanno vivendo. Così Federchimica e Farmindustria hanno condiviso con i sindacati(Filctem, Femca e Uiltec) il progetto di lanciare un’analisi sociale che verrà realizzata dall’Università degli Studi di Milano. L’obiettivo è aumentare l’attrattività del settore verso i talenti, gestire i bisogni di una forza lavoro in evoluzione e affrontare l’avvento delle nuove tecnologie. «Supportare la competitività delle nostre imprese significa saper comprendere in anticipo i fenomeni e i cambiamenti che incidono sulla società e, inevitabilmente, sul mondo del lavoro e sulla popolazione aziendale. Per svolgere in modo efficace il ruolo di parti sociali e continuare ad essere attrattivi senza perdere talenti, la strada è quella dell’ascolto e del confronto sulle aspettative di lavoratori e imprese», afferma il presidente di Federchimica, Francesco Buzzella. La domanda di competenze e le modalità organizzative del mondo del lavoro «stanno cambiando rapidamente, così come cambiano valori, aspettative soprattutto da parte delle nuove generazioni - ragiona il presidente di Farmindustria, Marcello Cattani -. L’industria farmaceutica vive di innovazione e ricerca ed è sensibile a questi cambiamenti, perché velocità di adattamento e risorse umane di eccellenza rappresentano i principali asset di competitività». Il modello di relazioni industriali del settore è ispirato da «dialogo, partecipazione e capacità di evolvere insieme, facendo del contratto non solo uno strumento regolatorio, ma una leva strategica per il futuro del settore».

Il progetto dell’indagine è nato proprio nell’ambito delle relazioni industriali e non ha precedenti a livello di settore. Verrà realizzata coinvolgendo direttamente imprese e lavoratori a cui verranno sottoposti due specifici questionari, studiati con il Dipartimento di Economia, Management e Metodi quantitativi (DEMM) dell’Università degli Studi di Milano. Saranno analizzate le caratteristiche della popolazione aziendale, oltre ai valori e alle aspettative di imprese e lavoratori, all’impatto dell’intelligenza artificiale, ai temi della rappresentanza e della partecipazione, esaminando anche le differenze generazionali e le varie dimensioni della diversità. I risultati dell’indagine diventeranno poi lo spunto degli Stati Generali delle Relazioni industriali di settore, che si svolgeranno nella primavera del 2027. L’evento sarà un momento di analisi e confronto sulle principali sfide dei prossimi anni: transizione digitale, intelligenza artificiale, nuovi modelli organizzativi, demografia e competenze, in un contesto di scenari geopolitici che impatta anche sul mondo del lavoro. L’obiettivo di imprese e sindacati è rafforzare la conoscenza di questi fenomeni per sostenere il ruolo centrale dell’impresa e delle relazioni industriali nel progresso della società, rispondendo così ai bisogni di crescita e benessere collettivi.
translated_text:
Per capire le trasformazioni del mercato del lavoro non resta che chiedere ai lavoratori e alle imprese come le stanno vivendo. Così Federchimica e Farmindustria hanno condiviso con i sindacati(Filctem, Femca e Uiltec) il progetto di lanciare un’analisi sociale che verrà realizzata dall’Università degli Studi di Milano. L’obiettivo è aumentare l’attrattività del settore verso i talenti, gestire i bisogni di una forza lavoro in evoluzione e affrontare l’avvento delle nuove tecnologie. «Supportare la competitività delle nostre imprese significa saper comprendere in anticipo i fenomeni e i cambiamenti che incidono sulla società e, inevitabilmente, sul mondo del lavoro e sulla popolazione aziendale. Per svolgere in modo efficace il ruolo di parti sociali e continuare ad essere attrattivi senza perdere talenti, la strada è quella dell’ascolto e del confronto sulle aspettative di lavoratori e imprese», afferma il presidente di Federchimica, Francesco Buzzella. La domanda di competenze e le modalità organizzative del mondo del lavoro «stanno cambiando rapidamente, così come cambiano valori, aspettative soprattutto da parte delle nuove generazioni - ragiona il presidente di Farmindustria, Marcello Cattani -. L’industria farmaceutica vive di innovazione e ricerca ed è sensibile a questi cambiamenti, perché velocità di adattamento e risorse umane di eccellenza rappresentano i principali asset di competitività». Il modello di relazioni industriali del settore è ispirato da «dialogo, partecipazione e capacità di evolvere insieme, facendo del contratto non solo uno strumento regolatorio, ma una leva strategica per il futuro del settore».
